description: G-d as One, Creator, Judge and Eternal; the Shekinah and its feminine aspects.
content_html:
The Nature of G-d in Judaism

Judaism is a monotheistic religion — Jews believe in one God alone. The word “God” is sometimes written as “G-d” in Jewish tradition as a mark of deep reverence, avoiding any risk of the divine name being treated disrespectfully. The most fundamental statement of Jewish belief about the nature of G-d appears in the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our G-d, the Lord is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). This affirmation of G-d’s oneness is the cornerstone of Jewish theology and is recited morning and evening.

Key Attributes of G-d

Jews understand G-d through several essential characteristics. G-d is described as Creator — the origin of all that exists. Genesis 1:1 opens with the declaration that “In the beginning G-d created the heavens and the earth,” establishing that the physical universe depends entirely on G-d for its existence. G-d is also understood as Eternal: unlike created beings, G-d has no beginning and no end and exists outside of time.

G-d is Law-Giver: Jewish tradition teaches that G-d communicated the Torah to Moses at Mount Sinai, providing the laws by which the Jewish people should live. Alongside this, G-d is Judge — the One who holds humanity accountable. On Rosh Hashannah, the New Year, Jews believe G-d judges the deeds of every person and determines what the coming year will hold. G-d is also All-powerful (omnipotent), All-knowing (omniscient), All-good (benevolent), and Everywhere (omnipresent).

Key Fact

Judaism teaches that G-d is One, Creator, Law-Giver, Judge and Eternal, as well as All-powerful, All-good, All-knowing and Everywhere. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the central declaration of G-d’s oneness and is the most important prayer in Jewish life.

Transcendent and Immanent

G-d is understood in Judaism as both transcendent — utterly beyond human comprehension and above the created universe — and immanent — close to and involved in the lives of human beings. Genesis 1:27 teaches that humans are created in the image of G-d, suggesting a relationship between the divine and humanity. This tension between transcendence and immanence is reflected throughout Jewish scripture and prayer.

G-d is described as “concerned with humanity” and “intervening” in history: the Exodus narrative shows G-d actively liberating the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Yet G-d’s nature also lies far beyond human understanding. The Book of Job explores how G-d’s ways can seem mysterious and beyond human reckoning, even while G-d remains just and good.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If G-d is all-powerful and all-good, why does evil and suffering exist? This is a profound question in Jewish thought. The Book of Job presents a righteous man who suffers terribly without apparent cause, raising the question of how G-d’s justice and goodness can be reconciled with human suffering. Jewish responses have varied: some emphasise that human free will allows for moral evil; others point to G-d’s justice working over longer timescales than humans can perceive; still others acknowledge that some suffering remains beyond full human understanding.

The Book of Job (which appears in the Jewish scriptures known as the Tenakh) presents G-d allowing Satan to test Job through terrible suffering. Job demands answers, and G-d responds by pointing to the incomprehensible vastness of creation, suggesting that human understanding is too limited to grasp divine purposes. The Book of Jonah illustrates a different aspect: G-d’s mercy even on enemies, showing that G-d’s judgement is tempered by compassion.

Orthodox Jewish thinkers have often emphasised that suffering can refine a person spiritually or serve as a test of faith. Progressive Jewish thinkers have sometimes moved away from seeing G-d as directly causing suffering, understanding G-d instead as a source of strength and comfort in difficult times. After the Holocaust, many Jewish theologians have engaged deeply with the question of whether belief in G-d’s justice and goodness can be maintained.

The Shekinah — G-d’s Manifest Presence

The Shekinah is a concept found in the Talmud and later Jewish writings. The word derives from the Hebrew root meaning “to dwell.” The Shekinah refers to the palpable, manifest presence of G-d dwelling among or near human beings — it is the “nearness” of G-d made tangible.

In the Hebrew scriptures, the Shekinah is described as appearing in the form of a cloud or pillar of fire. In Exodus 40:35, the cloud of G-d’s glory — the Shekinah — filled the Tabernacle so completely that even Moses could not enter. Similarly, Exodus 13:20–22 describes the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night that guided the Israelites through the wilderness. In Exodus 24:16, the glory of G-d settled on Mount Sinai like a cloud. Numbers 9:16 records that the cloud remained over the Tabernacle night and day throughout the Israelites’ wilderness journey.

Key Fact

The Shekinah is first used as a term in the Talmud (not the Hebrew Bible itself), and it refers to G-d’s manifest dwelling presence. It is associated with the cloud and pillar of fire in Exodus (Exodus 13:20–22; Exodus 40:35) and later became linked with ideas of G-d’s feminine aspects.

The Shekinah and the Feminine Aspects of G-d

In Jewish mystical and rabbinic thought, the Shekinah has often been understood as a feminine aspect of G-d. The Hebrew word “Shekinah” is grammatically feminine, and this has led thinkers in the Jewish mystical tradition (Kabbalah) to associate the Shekinah with the feminine dimension of the divine. In Kabbalistic thought, the divine nature is understood through ten attributes called the Sefirot. The Shekinah is associated with the lowest of these Sefirot, representing G-d’s immanent, creative and nurturing presence within the world.

There are different understandings of the Shekinah among Jewish thinkers. Some understand the Shekinah as synonymous with G-d — simply a way of speaking about G-d’s presence rather than a separate aspect of the divine. In this view, saying “the Shekinah dwells here” is the same as saying “G-d is present here.” This is the more mainstream rabbinic interpretation.

Others, particularly in Kabbalistic (Jewish mystical) tradition, see the Shekinah as G-d descending to dwell on Earth — a distinct emanation of the divine that bridges heaven and earth. Here the Sefirot explain how a transcendent G-d can be present within the created world. Some modern Jewish theologians use the Shekinah to explore the feminine dimension of the divine, challenging purely masculine language for G-d. More traditional (Orthodox) interpretation tends to resist seeing G-d as having a gender, understanding such language as metaphorical rather than literal.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on the nature of G-d, make sure you use the correct Jewish terminology: transcendent, immanent, omnipotent, omniscient, Shekinah and Rosh Hashannah. A common error is to confuse the Shekinah with a separate divine being — clarify that it means G-d’s manifest dwelling presence. For the 15-mark ‘Discuss’ question, always give arguments on both sides: for example, if asked whether the Shekinah shows G-d is immanent, consider both why it does (cloud/pillar of fire, dwelling among the Israelites) and whether the transcendent aspects of G-d challenge this view. Accurate spelling of technical terms like ‘Shekinah,’ ‘Sefirot,’ ‘omniscient’ and ‘transcendent’ is rewarded on extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Judaism is strictly monotheistic: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) declares G-d is One. G-d is understood as Creator, Law-Giver, Judge and Eternal, as well as all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good and everywhere present.
  • G-d is both transcendent (beyond creation) and immanent (involved in human life). The problem of evil, explored in the Book of Job, raises questions about G-d’s justice that Jewish thinkers have answered in different ways.
  • The Shekinah — a term first used in the Talmud — refers to G-d’s manifest presence. Associated with the cloud and fire in Exodus, it has also been linked in Jewish mystical thought (Kabbalah) with the Sefirot and the feminine aspects of G-d.

practice_questions.text: State the name of the Jewish declaration of faith that affirms G-d is One.
Describe what Jews mean when they say G-d is both transcendent and immanent.
practice_questions.marks: Transcendent: G-d exists beyond and outside the created world, above time and space [1 mark]. Immanent: G-d is also present within the world and involved in human lives, for example guiding the Israelites in the wilderness [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning and significance of the Shekinah in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: The Shekinah refers to G-d’s manifest or dwelling presence (1 mark); the term first appears in the Talmud, not the Hebrew Bible itself (1 mark); it is associated with the pillar of cloud and fire in Exodus (e.g. Exodus 40:35) (1 mark); in Kabbalistic thought it is linked with the Sefirot and the feminine aspects of G-d (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Jewish beliefs about the nature of G-d are expressed in scripture and tradition.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• G-d as One: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the central declaration of monotheism, recited daily; it affirms that G-d is absolutely singular and undivided, shaping all Jewish worship and identity.
• G-d as Creator: Genesis 1:1 states G-d created the heavens and the earth; this means the universe depends entirely on G-d and humans (Genesis 1:27 — made in G-d’s image) have a special relationship with the Creator.
• G-d as Judge: on Rosh Hashannah, Jews believe G-d evaluates each person’s deeds over the past year; this motivates Jews to repent and live righteously.
• The Shekinah: described in Exodus as the cloud filling the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:35), it represents G-d’s immanent presence; in Kabbalistic thought the Sefirot further explain how G-d interacts with the world.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per belief — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'The Shekinah proves that G-d is more immanent than transcendent in Judaism.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Shekinah describes G-d’s actual dwelling presence among the Israelites (Exodus 13:20–22; 40:35), suggesting closeness rather than distance.
• Kabbalistic understanding of the Sefirot places the Shekinah as G-d’s presence within the created world, emphasising immanence.
• Genesis 1:27 (humans created in G-d’s image) reinforces the idea of an intimate relationship between G-d and humanity.
• G-d’s intervention in history (the Exodus, giving the Torah) shows active involvement in human affairs.

Arguments against:
• The Shema and Jewish tradition strongly emphasise G-d’s absolute transcendence — G-d is beyond the universe, not contained within it.
• The Book of Job illustrates that G-d’s ways are incomprehensible to humans, suggesting distance rather than closeness.
• The Shekinah’s appearance as cloud and fire is itself a sign of G-d’s transcendence — G-d cannot be seen directly; only a manifestation is visible.
• Orthodox Judaism stresses that G-d is entirely unlike anything in creation and resists too much emphasis on immanence as potentially reducing G-d to a human scale.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 6:4; Exodus 40:35; Book of Job; Genesis 1:27), explicit weighing of which argument is stronger, justified conclusion noting the tension between immanence and transcendence as central to Jewish thought.
Secure: Clear arguments on both sides with some source reference; concludes with a reasoned judgement.
Developing: One side more developed than the other; some source reference; basic conclusion.
Emerging: Only one perspective given; little or no source reference; limited or no conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

practice_questions.text: Outline Jewish responses to the problem of evil and suffering.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Free will — G-d gave humans freedom, which allows moral evil (1 mark); the Book of Job shows G-d’s ways are beyond human understanding (1 mark); the Book of Jonah illustrates G-d’s mercy even toward wrongdoers (1 mark); some Jewish thinkers argue suffering can refine a person spiritually (1 mark); progressive Jewish theologians have revisited beliefs after the Holocaust (1 mark). [3 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that there is only one God.
The central Jewish declaration of faith, beginning 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our G-d, the Lord is One' (Deuteronomy 6:4).
Existing beyond the limits of time and space; without beginning or end.
One who evaluates human actions and determines consequences; in Judaism, G-d holds humanity accountable for their choices.
The Jewish New Year, a period of reflection during which G-d is believed to judge the deeds of each person.
Beyond and independent of the material world; existing outside time and space.
Present within and throughout the created world, involved in the lives of human beings.
The Hebrew Bible, consisting of the Torah (Law), Neviim (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).
The manifest presence of G-d, often associated with light or cloud; from the Hebrew root meaning 'to dwell'.
The body of Jewish oral law, commentary and discussion compiled by rabbinic scholars, supplementing the written Torah.
The ten divine powers or emanations through which, according to Jewish mystical thought, G-d interacts with the world.
